cues.text: Welcome to Chemical Thermodynamics.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Begin every energy calculation by choosing the system.
An open system exchanges matter and energy with its surroundings.
A closed system exchanges energy but not matter.
An isolated system exchanges neither.
Internal energy, enthalpy and entropy are state functions: their changes
depend
on initial and final states.
Heat and work describe energy transfer along a path.
Temperature and pressure are intensive properties; total volume and total
internal energy are extensive.
In the Chemistry convention, the first law is change in internal energy equals
heat plus work done on the system.
Heat entering is positive.
Compression work is positive, while expansion work is negative.
For expansion against a constant external pressure, work is minus external
pressure times the volume increase.
Consider a closed system that absorbs five hundred joules and expands by one
litre against two bar.
One litre bar equals one hundred joules.
The work is therefore minus two hundred joules, and the internal energy
increases by three hundred joules.
The system gained heat but returned some energy to the surroundings as work.
Notice that external pressure appears in this work expression.
If it varies, the appropriate pressure volume integral is needed.
Free expansion against zero external pressure does no pressure volume work.
Adiabatic means no heat transfer; it does not automatically mean constant
temperature.
Isothermal means constant temperature.
Isochoric means constant volume, and isobaric means constant pressure.
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, so an
isothermal
change has zero internal energy change even though heat and work may each be
nonzero.
Keep the signs tied to the chosen system, and always convert litre bar into
energy units before adding heat and work.
Enthalpy is defined as internal energy plus pressure times volume.
For a closed system undergoing only pressure volume work at constant pressure,
the heat transferred equals the enthalpy change.
At constant volume, with no other work, heat equals the internal energy
change.
The conditions are part of the result.
An exothermic process has a negative enthalpy change, while an endothermic
process has a positive one.
For ideal gaseous reactants and products at the same temperature, the gas
contribution gives change in enthalpy equals change in internal energy plus
change in gaseous mole number times R T.
In ordinary reaction calculations this form neglects condensed phase pressure
volume contributions.
Count only gaseous species when finding the gaseous mole change.
For one nitrogen plus three hydrogen forming two ammonia, all gases, the
change
is two minus four, or minus two moles per reaction as written.
Suppose the internal energy change is minus ninety point zero kilojoules for
that reaction amount at three hundred kelvin.
Use R equal to zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole
kelvin.
The correction is minus two times R times three hundred, about minus four
point
nine nine kilojoules.
The enthalpy change is about minus ninety five point zero kilojoules.
Reversing the reaction reverses both energy changes and the gaseous mole
change.
A separate useful relation for one mole of an ideal gas is molar heat capacity
at constant pressure minus molar heat capacity at constant volume equals R.
It is not a universal identity for liquids, solids or real gases.
Heat capacity relates heat to temperature change under specified conditions;
if
it varies appreciably with temperature, use an integral instead of a constant
value.
Check the phase labels and the reaction amount before substituting numbers.
Hess's law follows from enthalpy being a state function.
A reaction may be assembled from several steps; adding their enthalpy changes
gives the same overall change.
Reverse a step and reverse its sign.
Multiply an equation by a number and multiply its enthalpy by that number.
Here is an illustrative cycle.
Carbon as graphite plus oxygen forming carbon dioxide has enthalpy minus three
hundred ninety four kilojoules per mole of reaction.
Carbon monoxide plus half an oxygen forming carbon dioxide has enthalpy minus
two hundred eighty three.
We want graphite plus half an oxygen forming carbon monoxide.
Keep the first equation and reverse the second.
Carbon dioxide cancels, leaving the target reaction.
Add minus three hundred ninety four to plus two hundred eighty three to obtain
minus one hundred eleven kilojoules.
These rounded values illustrate the calculation; phases and reference
conditions must match.
Standard formation enthalpy refers to forming one mole of a substance from its
elements in their reference states.
The standard formation enthalpy of an element in its reference state is
assigned zero; this does not say that its internal energy or entropy is zero.
Multiply each formation enthalpy by its stoichiometric coefficient, then
subtract the reactant sum from the product sum.
Combustion enthalpy concerns complete burning of the specified amount, usually
one mole, with product phases stated.
Atomization creates gaseous atoms.
Sublimation converts solid to gas.
Ionization removes an electron from a gaseous species, while hydration brings
gaseous ions into water.
Dissolution can combine lattice separation and solvation effects.
For a gas phase bond estimate, add energies of bonds broken and subtract
energies of bonds formed.
Average bond enthalpies give an approximation because bond environments
differ.
Do not mix an average gas bond estimate with a liquid phase reaction without
accounting for phase changes.
Energy conservation alone does not choose the direction of a process.
Entropy supplies the second law criterion: a spontaneous change increases the
total entropy of the system and surroundings.
The system's entropy may decrease if the surroundings gain more.
A reversible ideal limit has zero total entropy production.
For a reversible isothermal path, entropy change is reversible heat divided by
temperature.
More generally, integrate reversible heat divided by temperature along a
suitable path between the states.
Entropy is a state function, even when the actual path is irreversible.
For the usual closed system at constant temperature and pressure, without
imposed non pressure volume work, a negative Gibbs energy change identifies a
thermodynamically favourable direction.
Gibbs energy change is enthalpy change minus temperature times entropy change.
Temperature must be in kelvin.
Match the energy units before subtracting.
Suppose enthalpy change is minus forty kilojoules and entropy change is minus
one hundred joules per kelvin.
Convert the entropy to minus zero point one zero zero kilojoules per kelvin.
At three hundred kelvin, Gibbs energy change is minus forty plus thirty, or
minus ten kilojoules.
At five hundred kelvin, it is minus forty plus fifty, or plus ten.
If both enthalpy and entropy changes are approximately temperature independent
over the range, the crossover is four hundred kelvin.
This exothermic process with decreasing entropy is favoured at lower
temperature.
Positive enthalpy and positive entropy favour higher temperature.
Negative enthalpy and positive entropy favour the forward direction throughout
the temperature range where those signs hold.
The opposite pair does not.
Finally, favourable does not mean fast.
A large activation barrier can make a thermodynamically favourable reaction
very slow.
Keep the direction question separate from the kinetics question.
The standard Gibbs energy change and the Gibbs energy change for the current
mixture are different quantities.
The connection is Gibbs energy change equals standard Gibbs energy change plus
R T times the natural logarithm of the reaction quotient Q.
The rigorous quotient uses dimensionless activities relative to standard
states.
For ideal dilute solutions and ideal gases, concentration or pressure ratios
provide useful approximations.
At equilibrium, the reaction Gibbs energy change is zero and Q equals the
equilibrium constant K.
Substitution gives standard Gibbs energy change equals minus R T times the
natural logarithm of K.
Thus a negative standard Gibbs energy change implies K greater than one at
that
temperature.
It does not guarantee that every possible mixture will proceed forward.
Take standard Gibbs energy change approximately minus five point seven four
four kilojoules per mole at three hundred kelvin.
With R equal to zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole
kelvin, the natural logarithm of K is about two point three zero three.
K is approximately ten.
If Q is one, the forward direction is favoured.
If Q is one hundred, Gibbs energy change is positive, about plus five point
seven four kilojoules per mole, and the reverse direction is favoured.
If Q is ten, the mixture is at equilibrium.
Combining the equations gives Gibbs energy change equals R T times the natural
logarithm of Q divided by K.
This directly connects composition to direction.
Standard conditions do not automatically mean two hundred ninety eight kelvin;
always read the stated temperature.
Finish with a short checklist: define the system, choose the correct work
sign,
preserve reaction coefficients and phases, convert entropy units, and
distinguish Q from K.
Use the worked notes and six original practice questions.
This is the core Unit four foundation; detailed enthalpy cycles, entropy
integrals and wider mixed problems remain for further study.
